1.text:
How Do Rocks Keep a Diary of 4.54 Billion Years?

Last deck, we traveled deep inside the Earth. Now we're going to read the rocks themselves, because rocks are a diary. They record volcanoes, oceans, swamps, ice sheets and even the day an asteroid ended the dinosaurs. Earth is 4.54 billion years old, and its rocks hold the story.

Here's the plan. Minerals are the building blocks, and rocks are made of minerals (or sometimes none at all). The rock cycle turns one kind of rock into another. Rocks also keep time: layers stack in order, radioactive atoms tick like clocks, and fossils mark the ages.

We'll finish with Indiana's own deep time. You'll find out that your state was once under a warm, shallow sea, then covered in swamps, and later buried under ice. Along the way we'll compare Earth with Mars, the Moon and meteorites.

Did you know? The oldest rocks you can hold in your hand didn't come from Earth. They fell from space.

2.text:
Today I Can...

Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of this deck. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

I can define a mineral and identify minerals by their properties in a lab. I can explain why a rock can hold many minerals, one mineral, or none. I can draw the rock cycle linking igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rock. I can model weathering, erosion, transport and deposition. I can date rocks by superposition, cross-cutting and half-life. I can build a timeline of how Indiana's sedimentary bedrock formed. I can show how seas, moving plates and ice reshaped Indiana.

Two more are enrichment goals that are part of this course. I can read the geologic time scale and use fossils as evidence. And I can compare Earth rocks with meteorites, Moon rocks and Mars rocks.

3.text:
What Makes a Mineral?

A mineral is a natural, inorganic solid with a set chemical makeup and an ordered crystal structure. Take it one word at a time. Natural means people didn't make it, so steel doesn't count. Inorganic means living things didn't make it. And an ordered crystal structure means its atoms line up in a neat repeating pattern, like tiles on a floor.

Minerals come in two flavors. Some are compounds, made of more than one element. Quartz, SiO2, is silicon and oxygen. Calcite, CaCO3, is calcium, carbon and oxygen, and it's Indiana's best-known mineral. Others are a single element, like gold, Au. The small numbers in a formula tell you how many atoms of each element there are.

More than 6,000 minerals are known. Because the atoms repeat the same way, a tiny grain of quartz sand has the same properties as a giant quartz crystal.

Did you know? Most minerals aren't pretty gems. The most common ones are ordinary, like the quartz in beach sand.

4.text:
What Is a Rock Made Of?

A rock is a natural solid of many minerals, one mineral, or none. Unlike a mineral, a rock doesn't have one formula or one crystal structure of its own. Think of minerals as ingredients and rocks as the dish.

Here are three Indiana examples. Shale is made of many minerals: tiny mud-sized grains of quartz plus other minerals. Limestone is made of one, mostly calcite. And coal is made of none, because it's mostly carbon from ancient plants. Since minerals can't be made by living things, coal doesn't count as a mineral.

Did you know? Limestone is a rock, not a mineral. It's a rock made mostly of the mineral calcite.

5.text:
Mineral Lab: Test, Don't Guess

Time to be a mineral detective. You'll test five samples, A through E, and fill in the table: color, streak, luster, hardness on the Mohs scale, and whether it fizzes in acid. Then name each mineral.

Here's your toolkit. Streak is the color of the powder a mineral leaves when you rub it on a rough porcelain plate. Luster is how the surface reflects light: metallic, glassy or dull. Hardness is how well a mineral resists scratching, from 1 (softest) to 10 (hardest) on the Mohs scale. Don't trust color alone. Many minerals come in several colors, and quartz comes in nearly every color there is.

Test each sample, fill the table, then name it. One last question to think about: which of these tests is chemical, and which are physical?

Did you know? "Hardness" in mineral terms doesn't mean how hard it is to break. It means how hard it is to scratch.

6.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Put the mineral rules to work. Which one is NOT a mineral?

Is it A) quartz, SiO2, B) calcite, CaCO3, C) coal from plants, or D) gold, Au? Go back to the definition on Slide 3 and test each choice against every part of it. Pick one and explain.

7.text:
One Rock Becomes Another

The rock cycle is rocks melting, weathering and changing into one another over time. There are three rock families, named by how they form.

Igneous rock forms when magma cools and hardens. Basalt, on the ocean floor, and granite, in the continents, are examples. Sedimentary rock forms when bits of older rock or shells get weathered loose, deposited, and cemented together. Sandstone, shale and limestone are sedimentary. Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change a rock without melting it. Quartzite is one example.

The main thing to remember: any rock can take any path. Any rock can melt into magma and cool into igneous rock. Any rock at the surface can weather into sediment. Any rock buried deep can be changed by heat and pressure. Most of these steps take millions of years.

Did you know? All of Indiana's bedrock is sedimentary. The only igneous and metamorphic rocks here were carried in by glaciers.

8.text:
From Mountain to Layer

How does a mountain turn into a layer of sandstone? Follow the steps. Step 1 is weathering, the breakdown of rock at Earth's surface. Physical weathering cracks rock into pieces. Chemical weathering changes the minerals, like iron rusting or calcite dissolving.

Step 2 is erosion, which moves the loose pieces away. Step 3 is transport, carrying them by water, wind or ice. Step 4 is deposition, where they drop out wherever the water slows down, in rivers, lakes and seas. The pieces settle by size and weight, building layers. Step 5 is compaction and cementing: buried sediment gets squeezed and glued together. Sand becomes sandstone, and mud becomes shale.

Weathering and erosion aren't the same thing. Weathering breaks rock; erosion moves it.

Did you know? In southern Indiana, slightly acidic rainwater dissolves limestone, making sinkholes, caves and springs. Near Mitchell, there are up to 1,023 sinkholes in a single square mile!

9.text:
Mars Kept Its Lake Beds

Mars has sedimentary rocks too, and they tell a story about water. Mudstone is rock made of hardened mud, often laid down in still water. Find mudstone, and you've found an old lake.

NASA's Curiosity rover explored Gale Crater. There, streams carried gravel and sand from the crater rim, and the finest mud settled on a lake floor, building layers. Wind later carved the crater fill into a mountain of layers called Mount Sharp, with lake mudstone at the base. Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater in 2021 and found the layers of an old river delta spilling out onto an old lake floor, just inside the crater rim.

Why are lake beds more than 3 billion years old still sitting on Mars's surface? Mars has no moving plates, so its crust doesn't get recycled the way Earth's does.

Did you know? Lake rocks on Mars mean it once had conditions that could have supported life. No life has been found there, though.

10.text:
Model It: The Rock Cycle

Time to draw two models. For Model A, make a rock cycle flowchart with igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rock. Show that every type can melt into magma, every type can weather into sediment, and every type can change by heat and pressure.

For Model B, make a sediment model. Show weathering (physical vs chemical), then erosion, transport and deposition, ending with new soil and sedimentary rock. Label one Indiana example.

Draw both models. Every arrow needs a process label. Watch out for a one-way circle: real rocks can jump between any of the three types.

11.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Follow a rock through the cycle. Basalt weathers, washes into a lake, gets buried and cemented. What is it now?

Is it A) sedimentary rock, B) metamorphic rock, C) igneous rock again, or D) magma? Trace each step on your rock cycle from Slide 10. Choose your answer and explain why it isn't the others.

12.text:
Which Layer Is Oldest?

Rocks don't come with birth certificates, but there are rules for putting them in order. The first is superposition: in undisturbed layers, the bottom layer is the oldest. Think of a pile of laundry. The shirt at the bottom went in first.

Look at the diagram. Layers A through E stack from oldest at the bottom to youngest at the top. Then there's F, a dike: a sheet of rock that cut across the other layers. That's the second rule, cross-cutting: whatever cuts across the layers must be younger than them. Dike F cuts A to D, so F is younger than those layers.

This kind of dating puts rocks in order without giving numbers in years. That's called relative dating. And don't let thickness fool you. The thickest layer isn't necessarily the oldest, because thickness says nothing about age.

Did you know? Most sediment is laid down flat. So if you see tilted layers, something moved them after they formed.

13.text:
Atomic Clocks

To get an actual age in years, geologists use radioactive atoms. A radioactive "parent" atom slowly changes into a stable "daughter" atom at a steady rate. The half-life is the time for half of the parent atoms to decay.

Follow the bar graph. At the start, 100% of the parent is there. After 1 half-life, 50% is left. After 2 half-lives, 25%. After 3 half-lives, 12.5%. Measure how much parent and daughter are in a crystal, and you can work out when it formed. Decay rates stay constant, which is why they work as clocks.

Different atoms tick at different speeds. Uranium-238 turns into lead-206 with a half-life of 4.5 billion years. Potassium-40 has a half-life of 1.25 billion years. About 89% of it turns into calcium-40 and about 11% into argon-40, the part geologists measure. Carbon-14 turns into nitrogen-14 in just 5,730 years, and it only works on once-living things, like wood or bone. That's why carbon-14 can't date dinosaur bones or ancient rocks.

Did you know? Carbon-14 only works for things from the last 50,000 years or so. After that, there's too little left to measure.

14.text:
The Oldest Rocks Fell From Space

Earth's age is 4.54 billion years. But here's a puzzle: no rock on Earth is that old. Follow the timeline, in billions of years ago, and see what we've found.

The oldest meteorite grains formed 4.567 billion years ago, right at the birth of the solar system. Earth forms at 4.54. The oldest Moon rocks are 4.4 to 4.5. The oldest Earth crystal, a tiny zircon from Australia, is 4.4 billion years old. The oldest Earth rock, the Acasta Gneiss in Canada, is 4.03. And Indiana's oldest exposed bedrock? Only about 0.45 billion years, or 450 million years.

Why is Earth's record so young? Plate tectonics recycles Earth's crust, sending old rock back into the mantle. The Moon and asteroids have no moving plates, so their ancient rocks survive. Scientists found Earth's age by comparing lead in Earth's oldest ores with lead in meteorites.

15.text:
Rocks From the Moon

Astronauts brought home quite a haul: 382 kg of Apollo samples from six Moon landings between 1969 and 1972. Those rocks tell the Moon's story.

The bright highlands are made of anorthosite: light rock made mostly of a mineral called plagioclase. It's 4.3 to 4.5 billion years old, and scientists think it floated to the top of an early ocean of melted rock. The dark maria are basalt lava, 3.2 to 3.9 billion years old, from later melting deep inside. Major volcanism ended about 3 billion years ago, and small eruptions continued until about 1 to 2 billion years ago.

Both kinds of Moon rock are igneous, like Earth's basalt and granite. But the Moon has almost no sedimentary rock, no running water and no plates. That's why its oldest crust survives.

Did you know? The dark maria were named "seas" long ago, but they hold no water. They're old lava plains.

16.text:
The Geologic Time Scale

To keep track of 4.5 billion years, geologists divide Earth's history into chunks, like chapters in a book. An eon is the largest division of geologic time. There are four: the Hadean, starting about 4,567 million years ago (Ma); the Archean, from 4,031 Ma; the Proterozoic, from 2,500 Ma; and the Phanerozoic, from 538.8 Ma to today.

The Phanerozoic, the eon of "visible life," splits into three eras. The Paleozoic runs from 538.8 to 251.9 Ma. The Mesozoic, the age of dinosaurs, runs from 251.9 to 66 Ma. The Cenozoic runs from 66 Ma to now.

Where does Indiana fit? Its exposed bedrock formed about 450 to 299 Ma, all in the Paleozoic. And the Ice Age covers the last 2.58 million years, a tiny sliver at the very end.

Did you know? The eons aren't equal. The Phanerozoic, with all its trilobites and dinosaurs, is less than 12% of Earth's history.

17.text:
Fossils Match the Layers

Fossils are evidence of past life: shells, teeth, bones, or traces like burrows and tracks. An index fossil is a fossil that marks rock of one age wherever it is found.

Here's how it works. The kinds of living things change over time, so the same fossils in different places mean the rocks are the same age. Look at site A and site B. Both have layers of brachiopods, trilobites and crinoids. Same fossils = same age, even though the sites are far apart.

Fossils also tell you about old environments. Brachiopods, trilobites and crinoids all lived in the sea, so rocks full of them formed underwater.

Did you know? Brachiopods look a lot like clams, but they aren't closely related. And Indiana's state fossil since 2022 is the American mastodon.

18.text:
Life Changed the Air

Today about 21% of the air is oxygen. But for roughly the first half of Earth's history, there was almost no free oxygen in the air at all.

That changed thanks to tiny ocean microbes called cyanobacteria. They made O2 by photosynthesis, the same way plants do today. About 2.4 billion years ago, oxygen built up in Earth's air for the first time: the Great Oxidation Event. With oxygen in the air, an ozone layer could form high up, which you'll learn about in Deck 11.

So the planet shaped life, and life shaped the planet right back. Microbes rewrote the whole planet's chemistry.

Did you know? The first oxygen didn't come from plants. Microbes made it, long before land plants existed.

19.text:
Five Mass Extinctions

Species die out all the time. A mass extinction is different: a short stretch of geologic time when a huge share of all species dies out. Earth has had five big ones.

The End-Ordovician, about 444 million years ago, wiped out 86% of species. The Late Devonian, about 372 million years ago, took 75%. The End-Permian, 251.9 million years ago, took 96%, the worst ever. The End-Triassic, about 200 million years ago, took 80%. The End-Cretaceous, 66 million years ago, took 76% and was the end of the dinosaurs.

After each one, survivors spread into the empty niches, the way mammals took over after the dinosaurs. That's why fossils change sharply at these layers, and why geologists draw period and era boundaries there.

Did you know? More than 99% of all species that ever lived are now extinct.

20.text:
An Asteroid Ends the Dinosaurs

66 million years ago, at the end of the Cretaceous, came the most famous extinction of all. Geologists call that moment the K-Pg boundary.

An asteroid about 10 to 20 km wide slammed into what is now the Yucatán in Mexico, leaving the Chicxulub crater, about 180 to 190 km wide. The sky went dark and the climate changed fast. 76% of species died, including all dinosaurs except birds. Afterward, mammals spread out and thrived.

What's the clue in the rock? A thin clay layer found worldwide, rich in iridium, a metal rare on Earth but common in asteroids.

Did you know? Birds are living dinosaurs, so the dinosaurs didn't completely disappear.

Check for Understanding: Part 3

Combine both kinds of dating. An ash layer in a stack of shale dates to 300 million years. What about the shale above it?

Is it A) younger than 300 million years, B) older than 300 million years, C) exactly 300 million years, or D) impossible to order? Use superposition from Slide 12 and the atomic clocks from Slide 13. Choose one and explain your reasoning.

22.text:
Indiana Under a Shallow Sea

Picture Indiana covered by a warm, shallow sea near the equator, full of strange sea creatures. That's what it was like for much of its ancient past. About 400 million years ago, plate motion had Indiana sitting near the equator under shallow water.

Look at the sea life on the slide: crinoids (sometimes called "sea lilies"), brachiopods, bryozoans and trilobites. When they died, their shell pieces piled up on the sea floor and hardened into limestone. Limestone is sedimentary rock made mostly of the mineral calcite, CaCO3. The shells are the limestone!

Indiana's most famous example is the Salem Limestone, about 340 million years old. This pure, thick limestone is a world-famous building stone. It built the Empire State Building, the Pentagon and 35 of the 50 state capitols.

Did you know? Indiana's limestone formed in a shallow sea, not a deep ocean.

23.text:
Coal From Ancient Swamps

Next chapter: swamps. During the Pennsylvanian period, 323 to 299 million years ago, southwestern Indiana was covered by swampy forests. Coal is carbon-rich rock made from buried plants.

Follow the steps. 1. A swamp forest grows. 2. Plants die and get buried. 3. Heat and pressure squeeze them over millions of years into a coal seam. All Indiana coal is bituminous, a middle grade of coal. Look for fossils of ferns, horsetails and lycopods (scaly-bark trees) near the coal.

Coal ties the rock cycle to the carbon cycle. Carbon that plants pulled from the air about 300 million years ago is locked inside the rock. When we burn coal, that carbon goes back into the air.

Did you know? Coal doesn't come from dinosaurs. It comes from plants, and Indiana's coal is older than the dinosaurs.

24.text:
The Ice Left a Blanket

The latest chapter of Indiana's story is ice. Over the past 2.6 million years, huge ice sheets crept down from Canada several times. The most recent one reached its farthest point 24,000 years ago, with its ice edge running across the middle of the state from Terre Haute to Brookville.

The glaciers scraped up bedrock to the north and dropped it as they melted. They left as much as 450 ft of glacial sediment over the bedrock. Much of it is till: an unsorted mix of boulders, pebbles, sand and clay dropped by ice. The ice also brought erratics: igneous and metamorphic rocks carried in from far away.

North of the ice edge are flat till plains. South of it are the Southern Hills, with rugged uplands and deep valleys that the last ice never reached.

Did you know? Glaciers don't only scrape away. They also dump thick blankets of sediment, and many Hoosiers drink groundwater from glacial sand and gravel.

25.text:
Timeline: Indiana in Deep Time

Now put the whole story together. Your timeline has five stops. About 450 Myr (million years) ago: an Ordovician sea. 340 Myr: a Mississippian sea builds the Salem Limestone. 323 to 299 Myr: Pennsylvanian coal swamps. After 299 Myr: no younger bedrock at all, a gap of nearly 300 million years. 24,000 years ago: Wisconsin ice drops till and erratics.

Add a diagram showing how Indiana moved: near the equator, then moving north as the plate carried it. Show sea level rising and falling, too.

Sketch each scene, then explain how seas, climate and ice shaped Indiana.

26.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 4

Test your sense of Indiana's history. Which list puts Indiana's history in order, oldest first?

Is it A) sea, then coal swamps, then glaciers, B) glaciers, then sea, then coal swamps, C) coal swamps, then glaciers, then sea, or D) sea, then glaciers, then coal swamps? Check your timeline from Slide 25. Pick one and explain.

27.text:
Exit Ticket

You read 4.54 billion years of history today. Show what you've learned with three questions.

First, why is calcite a mineral but coal is not? Second, trace a grain of sand from a mountain to an Indiana sandstone. Third, why are meteorites and Moon rocks older than any rock on Earth?

When you're done, look back at your "I can" list from Slide 2 and rate yourself again.

28.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask you to do, in plain words.

ES.5.1: run a lab to test minerals by their physical and chemical properties, and explain that rocks can hold many minerals, one or none, while minerals can be single elements like gold or compounds like silicates. ES.5.2: draw the rock cycle, showing how each rock type can melt, change by heat and pressure, or weather into sedimentary rock. ES.5.3: model the difference between weathering, erosion, transport, deposition and the making of new soil and sedimentary rock, and tell physical and chemical weathering apart.

ES.5.4: tell relative time from absolute time. Sedimentary rock is dated by its position, igneous rock by radioactive dating, and carbon dating is only for once-living things. ES.5.5: make a timeline of how Indiana's mostly sedimentary bedrock formed, and how seas, climate and glaciers shaped it. ES.5.6: model how moving plates and changing sea levels reshaped the continents, including inland seas, rock layers like evaporites and shell-built limestone, and the building and wearing away of landforms.
